extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent lawyers, judges, and practitioners assessing patentability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a proposed subject-matter (machine, manufacture, composition, design, or improvement) satisfies statutory and common-law criteria for patentability, including novelty, utility, and sufficiency of invention. Focuses on classification of subject-matter and tests for when an alleged change or improvement is substantial enough to support a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engine vs Method (mode referred to permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mode of doing a thing is referred to something permanent, it is properly termed an engine; when to something fugitive, a method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification affects whether the subject is treated as a machine/engine or as a method/process — useful for determining the kind of protection and statutory class under which the invention falls (cites Boulton v. Bull).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity of modus operandi
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry must be not whether the same elements or component parts are used, but whether the given effect is produced substantially by the same mode of operation and the same combination of powers in both machines; or whether some new element, combination, or feature has been added which produces either the same effect more cheaply or expeditiously, an entirely new effect, or an effect materially superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the mode of operation (modus operandi) and combination of powers rather than superficial component identity; changes producing cost/efficiency/quality improvements or new effects support patentability (cites Whittemore v. Cutter and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of a machine vs external resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the alleged improved machine operates upon the same principle as the former machine — i.e., whether it produces the same effect by the same mechanical means or by means substantially the same; external resemblance is not decisive because machines may appear similar but operate on different principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where doubt or complexity exists, consult skilled persons to ask whether the principles of two machines are the same or different; examples: lever vs screw vs pulley illustrate different principles despite superficial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When different effect is claimed, judge by character and importance of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the effect produced by the alleged invention is different, the test of a sufficient 'improvement' to sustain a patent will be the character and importance of the effect itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the new effect is materially important or valuable (e.g., better quality, new functionality), that supports patentability even if the change is small in structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-on-existing-patent claimability
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent including the subject-matter of a patent still in force is valid if the improvement only is claimed in the specification; the new patent will come into force after the expiration of the old one, or may be applied by using a license under the former patent or by purchasing the specific machine covered by the former patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical options include waiting for expiration, obtaining a license, or purchasing the patented apparatus; courts require the former patent specification to be read in infringement suits alleging improvements (cites Crane v. Price and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture: definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'manufacture' denotes any thing made by the hand of man; it embraces machinery as well as substances or fabrics produced by art and industry, and may include processes of making a thing where the vendible substance is the subject of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In English law 'manufacture' is broad; under some statutory constructions it may be limited to vendible articles (fabrics/substances) rather than machinery. The essential point is that the subject matter be a vendible article or a result produced by art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for classifying an article as manufacture vs machine
rubrics_metrics.description: If the article is produced and intended to be sold and used separately as a merchantable commodity and its merit consists in being a better article or produced by a cheaper process, it may be considered a manufacture; but if its merit appears only after incorporation with some mechanism and consists in producing a new effect when combined, it should be regarded as a machine or improvement of a machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification should follow the practical use and the source of the merit (merchantable standalone article vs component whose advantage appears only in combination with mechanism). The exact label is not vital to validity so long as the thing is correctly described and meets novelty and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter: novelty of combination
rubrics_metrics.description: For compositions the test of novelty is not whether the materials are new but whether the combination is new; different proportions or addition of other ingredients can make a valid composition patent even if ingredients were previously in common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent may cover both the new composition itself and the process of making it, but if only the process is new and the article not new, the patent is for the art/process rather than a composition-of-matter patent (cites Ryan v. Goodwin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents — subject-matter and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for designs (new and original designs for manufactures, ornaments, prints, pictures, or new useful and original shapes/configurations of articles of manufacture) are authorized by statute; applicants may elect terms (3.5, 7, or 14 years) and general patent regulations apply so far as consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs are distinct statutory subject-matter with specific term options; follow statutory provisions (Acts of 1842, 1861, and 1870 §71, §76).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requisites: novelty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the discovery or invention of any new and useful art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement on any of these things, which the statute makes the subject of a patent; novelty and utility are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before other qualitative inquiries, confirm the subject belongs to a statutory class and that the claimed subject is both new (novel) and useful (utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention not measured by effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of invention does not depend on the quantity of thought, ingenuity, skill, labor, or money expended; whether the invention was the result of long experiment or accidental discovery is not the essential ground of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law looks to character of the result rather than the inventor's mental process; however, the possibility that skill or design could have been exercised may be relevant to showing substantial novelty (cites Crane v. Price, Earle v. Sawyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility-of-design test (exercise of inventive faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the law does not regard the mental process by which the invention was produced as decisive, it may require that the result be such as not to exclude the possibility that some skill or ingenuity was exercised; if the character of the alleged invention is such that no design or study could possibly have been exercised, that tends to show it does not differ substantially from what existed before or is frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test where character of the product might exclude the possibility of study or design; it is an indirect means to infer substantial novelty rather than a formal requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frivolousness and mere colorable variations are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute frivolous and foolish inventions, though novel in one sense, are not patentable; mere colorable variations or slight and unimportant changes, or employment of an obvious substitute, will not support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: immersing cloth in a steam-bath instead of hot water, substituting steam to heat rollers instead of hot iron bars — if consequences are unimportant, the change is treated as colorable variation or double use and not substantive invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative utility/importance test for sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If the result produced by a combination is a new article, a better article, or a cheaper article to the public than the old method produced, such a combination is an invention or manufacture intended by the statute and may be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the change was accidental, significant practical utility or important consequences (e.g., cheaper/better production) demonstrate sufficiency of invention (examples: Crane, Neilson, Dudley, Hall, Derosne). If change is immaterial and produces no benefit, it will not support a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-invention test: improvement judged by result
rubrics_metrics.description: When a machine or combination of machinery is claimed, the gist of the objection often is whether the alleged new machinery serves the purpose better than the machinery formerly used; utility and improved performance are decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actual improvement in functioning or durability (example Brunton's chain-link and anchor cases — one part supported because substitution was materially beneficial; the other part failed because it was simple application of known mode and produced no superiority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change plus consequences must be judged together
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of invention sufficient to support a patent may be estimated from a compound view of the change effected and the consequences of that change; both taken together must be considerable/important to satisfy sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight structural change can still be patentable if it leads to important practical results; conversely, small change with minor consequences fails. View change and results as a sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be a thing made or an art/process
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no valid patent except it be for a thing made, or for the art or process of making or doing something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract ideas or things not made nor usable in a process fall outside patentability; ensure claim scope describes a concrete thing or a process of making/doing.
